# Curvature-potential locality on a singular support

This strengthens the first-order conclusion of
`candidate ed7be0e1efdfe13b`. It is local on an interval with
stable support compatibility and fixed strict cap memberships. It does not
remove that stability requirement or manufacture a common curvature source.

## 1. A one-dimensional locality lemma

Let F be locally absolutely continuous on an open interval, with derivative
g=F' of locally bounded variation. Let E be a relatively closed set on which
F is zero. Then the diffuse part of the measure F''+F dtheta vanishes on E.

Here diffuse means the measure with all its point atoms removed. A BV
function has left and right limits everywhere and is continuous except at
its countably many jump points, after choosing the usual precise
representative. At every continuity point x of g, the identity
F(y)-F(x)=integral_x^y g implies that F is differentiable at x with derivative
g(x). If x is also a nonisolated point of E, taking y in E tending to x
shows g(x)=0. The isolated points of E and the jump points of g are
countable and therefore irrelevant to diffuse measures.

For completeness, the BV locality fact used here is

    D^c g restricted to {x:g is continuous at x and g(x)=0} = 0.       (1)

One proof uses T_epsilon(t)=epsilon arctan(t/epsilon). The one-dimensional
BV chain rule reads

    D(T_epsilon(g))
      = T_epsilon'(g) D^c g
        + sum_x [T_epsilon(g(x+))-T_epsilon(g(x-))] delta_x.

This chain rule follows first for continuous BV functions by applying the
mean-value identity to partitions, using uniform continuity of T' on the
bounded range of g, and then passing to the variation-measure limit. For a
general BV function, remove its jump intervals in the graph and apply that
continuous argument to the remaining graph; the contribution of each
removed interval is exactly the displayed endpoint difference. Equivalently,
finite-jump approximations plus the summable total jump variation give the
same identity. Thus the formula involves no untracked choice of point value
at a jump.

The functions T_epsilon(g) converge uniformly to zero, so their distributional
derivatives converge to zero. On the diffuse term,
T_epsilon'(t)=epsilon^2/(epsilon^2+t^2) is bounded by1 and tends to the
indicator of t=0. Dominated convergence applies against the finite total
variation of D^c g on compact intervals. Each jump difference tends to zero
and is bounded in absolute value by |g(x+)-g(x-)|; those bounds are summable.
The jump measures therefore converge to zero in total variation. This proves
(1), by testing against arbitrary continuous compactly supported functions.
It follows that D^c g restricted to E vanishes. Since F=0 on E, so does
F dtheta restricted to E, proving the lemma.

## 2. Potentials annihilated by common-curvature source tests

Let mu be a finite signed measure on [a,b], and let nu be a nonzero finite
nonatomic measure supported inside (a,b). Write E=supp(nu), and define

    U(s)=integral_[s,b] sin(theta-s) dmu(theta).

For every bounded psi satisfying the two moment conditions

    integral psi sin(s) dnu(s)=integral psi cos(s) dnu(s)=0,

assume

    integral psi(s) U(s) dnu(s)=0.                         (2)

Then the diffuse part of mu vanishes on E.

Indeed the linear functional psi -> integral psi U dnu vanishes on the
kernel of the map psi -> (integral psi sin dnu, integral psi cos dnu).
It therefore factors through the image of that map, a subspace of R^2.
Extending the resulting linear functional to R^2 gives constants A,B with
U=A sin+B cos nu-almost everywhere. The function U is continuous, so this
identity holds everywhere on E. Set F=U-A sin-B cos. Its derivative is BV,
and distributionally

    F''+F dtheta=mu.

Apply Section1. No assumption that E contains an interval, or that nu has
full support on (a,b), has been used.

## 3. Consequence for the common-curvature stress

In `candidate ed7be0e1efdfe13b`, fix v in the admissible kernel
L (or the partial-source kernel L_J), and put

    mu_v = sum_z W_z v_z R_z.

The first-order stress annihilates every admissible Green-potential
acceleration. Orthogonality to the first area moments is not imposed for
these acceleration tests; only the two gluing moments are required. Fubini
therefore gives exactly (2). Consequently

    (sum_z W_z v_z R_z)^c restricted to supp(nu) = 0        (3)

for every v in the same kernel. This conclusion strengthens annihilation
against the potential tests to an actual measure identity on the support of
the common nonatomic curvature source. A finite basis of the kernel suffices
to make all identities simultaneous.

The existing disjoint-source construction also provides

    sum_z W_z v_z^2 >= 0   for every v in that kernel.

Combining this with (3), and taking densities relative to the total diffuse
curvature measure restricted to supp(nu), yields the corresponding nullspace
condition whenever that density vector belongs to the same kernel. In the
full-source case this follows from the identically active support relations.
For a partial-source kernel, curvature of indices outside J can still occur
on supp(nu); one must not silently put those coordinates to zero. Equation
(3), without such an extra membership assertion, remains valid.

This local result does not control curvature supported on unstable contact
sets, purely atomic curvature, or mutually singular sources with no nonzero
compatible signed direction.
